messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cybersecurity Analyst
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Bao presents as a quiet, meticulously dressed man of 75, whose precision as a cybersecurity analyst seems at odds with the disarray he describes in his own mind. For nearly fifty years, he had managed to contain the memories of his firstborn son’s brief, harrowing life. Now, following the recent death of his wife, the containment has failed. The story emerges in fragments, the narrative thread often breaking mid-sentence as he loses his place, staring at a point on the wall as if watching a scene only he can see.

It was 1974. His son, Minh, was born seemingly healthy, but within hours, a terrifying blueness crept into his skin. What followed was a blur of frantic activity in the neonatal intensive care unit. The memory that haunts Bao is not a cohesive story but a series of sensory snapshots that play on a relentless loop. He can still feel the cold vinyl of the waiting room chair, smell the sharp, chemical clean of the floor polish that seemed to permeate everything, and see the flickering fluorescent lights of the hallway. The most vivid part of this internal film is the image of Minh in the incubator, a tiny, fragile body lost in a tangle of wires and tubes, his chest rising and falling with the rhythmic sigh of the ventilator. Bao remembers the hushed, grave tones of the doctors, the medical jargon he couldn't grasp, and a profound, suffocating sense of helplessness.

For decades, these memories were ghosts, present but manageable. Now, they are solid, immediate threats. At his office, a younger colleague recently announced his wife’s pregnancy with joyful photos of an ultrasound. As the team gathered to congratulate him, the cheerful office chatter faded for Bao. A phantom scent of antiseptic filled his nostrils, sharp and cloying. His heart began to hammer against his ribs, a frantic, painful rhythm. He felt a sudden, dizzying sense of dislocation, the modern glass-and-steel office dissolving around him, replaced by the pale green walls of the hospital. For a terrifying moment, he was certain he was back there, standing uselessly beside the incubator. He mumbled an excuse and fled to the restroom, splashing cold water on his face until the present day reasserted itself. Since then, he has avoided the colleague, taking his lunch at his desk and finding reasons to work from home, a decision that has created a noticeable distance between him and his team.

Bao has come to believe that his own emotional reactions are dangerous. The wave of guilt that washes over him—the unanswerable question of whether he should have done something different, something more—feels like a physical force that could overwhelm him entirely. This fear of his own feelings has become a prison. He recently received a notice for a routine cardiac check-up, a necessity at his age. The thought of the examination—the sterile room, the medical equipment, the simple act of being a patient—is paralyzing. He is convinced that if he goes, the experience will trigger a complete collapse, that the film in his head will start and this time, it will not stop.

When his daughter, now a mother herself, tries to talk to him about his grief for his late wife, Bao finds he cannot articulate what is truly happening. He will start to explain the fear, the intrusive images, but the words get tangled. He loses the thread, trailing off as the memory pulls him back, feeling not like a recollection from the distant past but like an event happening in the present moment. It was his daughter’s insistence, her gentle but firm observation that he was disappearing into himself, that finally prompted him to seek help. He sits in the therapy room, his hands clasped tightly in his lap, admitting that his greatest hope is simply to be able to attend his grandson’s upcoming birthday party without the fear that the sight of a child’s joy will plunge him back into the silent, sterile horror of the hospital ward.
